items.q: How is the fee determined under a cost-plus-incentive-fee contract?
items.a: It is a cost-reimbursement contract with a target cost, target fee, minimum and maximum fees, and a formula that adjusts the fee based on total allowable costs versus target costs; outside the formula range the contractor receives allowable costs plus the minimum or maximum fee.

cite.quote: The cost-plus-incentive-fee contract is a cost-reimbursement contract that adjusts the initially negotiated fee based on a formula comparing total allowable costs to total target costs. This contract type includes a target cost, target fee, minimum and maximum fees, and a fee adjustment formula.

items.q: What two pieces make up the fee on a cost-plus-award-fee contract?
items.a: A base amount fixed at inception (if used, at the contracting officer's discretion) and an award fee the contractor may earn in whole or in part to motivate excellence in cost, schedule, and technical performance — decided each evaluation period by the Fee-Determining Official on the Award-Fee Board's recommendations. DoD adds hard guardrails: base fee capped at 3 percent of the estimated cost exclusive of fee, at least 40 percent of the award fee held for the final evaluation (going lower takes nondelegable HCA approval), award-fee payments outside the end-of-period evaluation prohibited, and the FDO's rating due to the contractor within 45 calendar days of the end of the period.

cite.quote: A cost-plus-award-fee contract is a cost-reimbursement contract that provides a fee consisting of (1) a base amount fixed at inception of the contract, if applicable and at the discretion of the contracting officer, and (2) an award fee that the contractor may earn in whole or in part to provide motivation for excellence in the areas of cost, schedule, and technical performance.

dod.quote: The base fee must not exceed three percent of the estimated cost of the contract exclusive of the fee.

items.q: By when must a UCA's definitization schedule provide for definitization?
items.a: By the earlier of 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal, or the date obligated funds exceed 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price. The 180 days runs from the qualifying proposal — not from award.

cite.quote: UCAs must contain definitization schedules that provide for definitization by the earlier of— (1) The date that is 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal.

items.q: How much of a UCA's not-to-exceed price may be obligated before definitization?
items.a: No more than 50 percent — raised to no more than 75 percent if the contractor submits a qualifying proposal before 50 percent has been obligated.

cite.quote: The Government must not obligate more than 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price before definitization. However, if a contractor submits a qualifying proposal before 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price has been obligated by the Government, then the limitation on obligations before definitization may be increased to no more than 75 percent

items.q: What definitization schedule applies to a DoD letter contract?
items.a: The UCA schedule at 217.7404-3(a): definitize by the earlier of 180 days after the contractor submits a qualifying proposal (extendable up to 90 more days only by HCA-level written determination) or the point where obligations exceed 50 percent of the not-to-exceed price. R-DFARS 216.603-2(c) applies that schedule instead of the civilian baseline at 16.603-2(c) — 180 days from the letter contract or 40 percent of the work — so for a DoD contracting officer the baseline rule simply does not apply.

cite.quote: In accordance with 10 U.S.C. 3372, establish definitization schedules for letter contracts following the requirements at 217.7404-3(a) instead of the requirements at FAR 16.603-2(c).

items.q: A UCA definitizes after the 180-day window from the qualifying proposal has run. What does that do to the contractor's profit?
items.a: Normally the profit on a late-definitized UCA reflects the contractor's reduced cost risk for costs already incurred. But when the contracting officer definitizes after the 180-day period from the qualifying proposal, the allowed profit must accurately reflect the contractor's cost risk as it existed on the date the qualifying proposal was submitted — the Government's own delay cannot be used to ratchet profit down further. The HCA ensures it, and the risk assessment is documented in the price negotiation memorandum.

cite.quote: the profit allowed on the contract must accurately reflect the cost risk of the contractor as such risk existed on the date the contractor submitted the qualifying proposal

items.q: R-DFARS splits its LPTA restrictions into limitations and prohibitions. What falls on each side of the line?
items.a: Limitations — avoid to the maximum extent practicable: acquisitions predominantly for information technology, cybersecurity, systems engineering and technical assistance, advanced electronic testing, or other knowledge-based professional services; personal protective equipment generally; and knowledge-based training or logistics services in contingency or other overseas operations. Prohibitions — do not use, period: PPE or aviation critical safety items where quality failure could cause combat casualties; engineering and manufacturing development for a major defense acquisition program; and auditing services. Mixing the two lists is the classic board trap — "avoid" is judgment, "do not use" is absolute.

cite.quote: Avoid using the lowest price technically acceptable source selection approach, to the maximum extent practicable, for acquisitions that are predominately for— (i) Information technology services, cybersecurity services, systems engineering and technical assistance services, advanced electronic testing, or other knowledge-based professional services; (ii) Items designated by the requiring activity as personal protective equipment (except see paragraph (b)(1) of this section); or (iii) Services designated by the requiring activity as knowledge-based training or logistics services in contingency operations or other operations outside the United States. (b) Prohibitions. Do not use the lowest price technically acceptable source selection approach to procure— (1) Items designated by the requiring activity as personal protective equipment or as an aviation critical safety item, for which the level of quality or failure of the equipment or item could result in combat casualties.

items.q: The Government decides it will pay any fair and reasonable price for the highest quality performance, with no tradeoffs. What source selection approach is that, and how does award actually work?
items.a: Highest technically rated with a fair and reasonable price. All proposals are evaluated on the non-price factors in the solicitation; the source selection authority identifies the highest technically rated proposal and only then evaluates that proposal's price for fair-and-reasonableness under subpart 15.4. If the price passes, that proposal is selected — no tradeoffs. If it does not, the SSA moves to the next highest technically rated proposal and repeats until award. The RFP must tell offerors up front that tradeoffs between price and non-price factors will not be considered.

cite.quote: If the highest technically rated proposal’s price is fair and reasonable, the proposal is selected for award. If the price is not fair and reasonable, the source selection authority must determine the next highest technically rated proposal and evaluate whether the price is fair and reasonable in accordance with subpart 15.4. This process continues until a contract is awarded to the highest technically rated responsible offeror with a fair and reasonable price.

items.q: Who is the source selection authority by default, and what must the SSA lock down before the RFP goes out?
items.a: The contracting officer is the SSA unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions. Before RFP release the SSA approves the source selection approach or acquisition plan, and establishes an evaluation team tailored to the acquisition with contracting, legal, logistics, technical, and other expertise. The SSA must ensure proposals are evaluated solely on the RFP's factors and subfactors, and may reject all proposals when that serves the Government's best interest. In DoD, high-dollar acquisitions also require SSA approval of a source selection plan before the solicitation issues.

cite.quote: Agency heads are responsible for source selection. A contracting officer is designated as the source selection authority (SSA), unless the agency head appoints another individual for a particular acquisition or group of acquisitions.

dod.quote: For high-dollar value and other acquisitions, as prescribed by agency procedures, the source selection authority must approve a source selection plan before the solicitation is issued.

items.topic: Certified Cost or Pricing Data & Proposal Analysis
items.q: How are forward pricing rate agreement rates used once established?
items.a: As the bases for pricing all contracts, modifications, and other contractual actions performed during the period the agreement covers; conditions affecting the agreement's validity must be promptly reported to the administrative contracting officer. In DoD the rates are not optional: use FPRA rates whenever they are available unless the head of the contracting activity waives them on a case-by-case basis — and advise the ACO of each case waived.

cite.quote: Contracting officers will use FPRA rates as bases for pricing all contracts, modifications, and other contractual actions to be performed during the period covered by the agreement.

dod.quote: Use forward pricing rate agreement (FPRA) rates when such rates are available, unless waived on a case-by-case basis by the head of the contracting activity.

items.q: What are DoD's customary progress payment rates — and when should progress payments not be the first choice?
items.a: 80 percent for large business concerns and 90 percent for small business concerns — the same rates apply to contracts carrying foreign military sales requirements. Progress payments are not the default, though: performance-based payments are the preferred financing method when practical and the contractor agrees, and in DoD they must be conditioned on the achievement of performance outcomes, never on costs incurred.

cite.quote: The customary progress payment rates for DoD contracts, including contracts that contain foreign military sales (FMS) requirements, are 80 percent for large business concerns and 90 percent for small business concerns.

items.q: When is a cost "reasonable," and who carries the burden when the contracting officer challenges one?
items.a: A cost is reasonable if, in nature and amount, it does not exceed what a reasonable person in the conduct of competitive business would incur. No presumption of reasonableness attaches merely because the cost was incurred — and if the contracting officer or the contracting officer's representative challenges a specific cost, the burden of proof is on the contractor to prove the cost is reasonable.

cite.quote: A cost is reasonable if, in its nature and amount, it does not exceed that which would be incurred by a reasonable person in the conduct of competitive business. (1) No presumption of reasonableness must be attached to the incurrence of costs. (2) If the contracting officer, or the contracting officer’s representative, challenges a specific cost, the burden of proof is on the contractor to prove that the cost is reasonable.

items.q: When does the Government get unlimited rights in technical data?
items.a: When the item, component, or process was or will be developed exclusively with Government funds — plus categories like form, fit, and function data; data necessary for installation, operation, maintenance, or training purposes other than detailed manufacturing or process data (that OMIT carve-out is the most-fought-over line in DoD data rights — dropping it flips the answer); and publicly available data.

cite.quote: The Government obtains unlimited rights in technical data, computer software, or computer software documentation that are— (1) Technical data related to an item, component, or process which has been or will be developed exclusively with Government funds; (2) Studies, analyses, test data, or similar data produced in the performance of a contract when the study, analysis, test, or similar work was specified as an element of performance; (3) Created exclusively with Government funds in the performance of a contract that does not require the development, manufacture, construction, or production of items, components, or processes; (4) Form, fit, and function data; (5) Necessary for installation, operation, maintenance, or training purposes (other than detailed manufacturing or process data);

items.q: Mixed Government and private funding produced the technical data. What rights arise, and for how long?
items.a: Government purpose rights. The period is negotiable with a five-year period nominal, and it begins upon execution of the contract, subcontract, or similar instrument that required the development — not at delivery. When it expires the Government's rights become unlimited, including the right to authorize others to use the data or software for commercial purposes.

cite.quote: The period during which government purpose rights are effective is negotiable. A five year period is nominal. Either the Government or the contractor may request a different period. (3) The government purpose rights period begins upon execution of the contract, subcontract, or similar contractual instrument that required the development. Upon expiration of the Government rights period, the Government has unlimited rights in the data or software including the right to authorize others to use the data or software for commercial purposes.

items.q: Development was exclusively at private expense. What rights does the Government get in the technical data versus the noncommercial software?
items.a: Limited rights in the technical data; restricted rights in the noncommercial computer software. Limited rights data cannot be used, released, or disclosed outside the Government without the asserting contractor's permission — except when necessary for emergency repair and overhaul, to a covered Government support contractor, or to a foreign government (other than detailed manufacturing or process data) for evaluational or informational purposes in the interest of the United States.

cite.quote: Do not use, release, or disclose data in which the Government has limited rights outside the Government without the permission of the contractor asserting the restriction except when it is— (i) Necessary for emergency repair and overhaul; (ii) To a covered Government support contractor; or (iii) To a foreign government, other than detailed manufacturing or process data, when use, release, or disclosure is in the interest of the United States and is required for evaluational or informational purposes.

items.q: Delivered technical data arrives marked with restrictive legends the program doubts. What is the Government's recourse, and how long does it have?
items.a: A contractor's assertions do not, by themselves, determine the Government's rights. Review asserted restrictions before accepting the deliverable, and the contracting officer may challenge an assertion when reasonable grounds exist to believe it is invalid — within six years after final payment or six years after delivery of the data or software, whichever is later. Commercial products are presumed developed exclusively at private expense, so challenging one takes specifically stated reasonable grounds; and a contractor's failure to respond to a challenge notice cannot be the sole basis for a final decision denying the restriction.

cite.quote: Challenge assertions within six years after final payment under the contract or six years after delivery of the data or software, whichever is later.

items.q: A contractor helped write the work statement for a competitive services acquisition. May it compete to perform the services?
items.a: Not generally. A contractor that prepares or assists in preparing the work statement may not supply the system or services unless it is the sole source, it participated in the development and design work, or more than one contractor was involved in preparing the work statement.

cite.quote: that contractor may not supply the system, major components of the system, or the services unless— (i) It is the sole source; (ii) It has participated in the development and design work; or (iii) More than one contractor has been involved in preparing the work statement.

items.q: The agency wants to waive an OCI rule. Who can, and how far down may that authority travel?
items.a: The agency head or a designee may waive any general rule or procedure of the OCI subpart by determining that its application in the particular situation would not be in the Government's interest. The request must be in writing and set forth the extent of the conflict — and waiver authority must not be delegated below the head of a contracting activity.

cite.quote: Agency heads must not delegate waiver authority below the level of head of a contracting activity.

items.q: How long does the contracting officer have to issue a final decision on a certified claim over $100,000?
items.a: 60 days after receiving the certified claim — or, within those 60 days, notify the contractor of the time within which a decision will be issued. One senior-level escape hatch: if a claim over $100,000 carries a defective certification, the contracting officer has no obligation to render a final decision at all, provided the contractor is notified in writing, within 60 days of receiving the claim, of the reasons the attempted certification was found defective.

cite.quote: For claims over $100,000, 60 days after receiving a certified claim; provided, however, that if a decision will not be issued within 60 days, the contracting officer must notify the contractor, within that period, of the time within which a decision will be issued.

items.q: After a contracting officer's final decision, what are the contractor's appeal routes and deadlines?
items.a: Appeal to the agency board of contract appeals within 90 days of receiving the decision, or bring an action directly in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims within 12 months.

cite.quote: you may bring an action directly in the United States Court of Federal Claims (except as provided in 41 U.S.C. 7102(d), regarding Maritime Contracts) within 12 months of the date you receive this decision

items.q: The contracting officer never issues a decision within the required time. What happens to the claim?
items.a: The failure is deemed a decision denying the claim, and it authorizes the contractor to file an appeal or suit.

cite.quote: Any failure of the contracting officer to issue a decision within the required time periods will be deemed a decision by the contracting officer denying the claim and will authorize the contractor to file an appeal or suit on the claim.

items.q: A contractor's failure (other than late delivery) is endangering performance before the delivery date. What notice applies?
items.a: A cure notice: written notice specifying the failure and allowing at least 10 days (or longer if necessary) to cure it before the Government may terminate for default.

cite.quote: (1) Give the contractor written notice specifying the failure; (2) Allow 10 days (or longer if necessary) to cure the failure

items.q: When is a show cause notice used instead of a cure notice?
items.a: When the time remaining in the delivery schedule will not permit a realistic cure period of 10 days or more — typically once delivery is already delinquent. It is sent immediately upon expiration of the delivery period and asks the contractor to show why the contract should not be terminated for default.

cite.quote: If the time remaining in the contract delivery schedule is not sufficient to permit a realistic "cure" period of 10 days or more, the following "Show Cause Notice" may be used. It should be sent immediately upon expiration of the delivery period.

items.q: Before issuing a default termination the contracting officer determines the failure was excusable. Now what?
items.a: Default termination is off the table. If termination is still in the Government's interest, terminate for convenience instead.

cite.quote: If the contracting officer determines before issuing the termination notice that the failure was excusable, they must not terminate for default. If termination is still in the Government's interest, they may terminate for convenience.

items.q: The Government terminates a contract for convenience. How does the contractor get paid, and on what clock?
items.a: Through settlement with the termination contracting officer. The final settlement proposal is due within one year of the termination date unless the TCO allows more time, and it covers all cost elements including subcontract settlements and proposed profit. The TCO negotiates a fair and prompt settlement where possible, settling by determination only when agreement fails; a no-cost settlement closes it out when no costs were incurred or the contractor waives them and nothing is owed the Government. Partial payments may flow before settlement when the contract authorizes them. And if a default termination is later found improper or excusable, the parties' rights and obligations convert to those of a convenience termination.

cite.quote: The final settlement proposal must be submitted within one year from the termination date, unless the TCO allows more time.

items.q: Transfers of Government contracts are statutorily prohibited. When does recognizing a successor in interest require a novation agreement — and when is a novation unnecessary?
items.a: A novation is the vehicle when it is in the Government's interest and the third party's interest arises from the transfer of all the contractor's assets, or the entire portion involved in performing the contract. It is unnecessary for a change in ownership by stock purchase with no legal change in the contracting party, where that party remains in control of the assets and keeps performing — the ownership changed, the contractor did not. A name-only change with rights and obligations unaffected takes a change-of-name agreement instead.

cite.quote: A novation agreement is unnecessary when there is a change in the ownership of a contractor as a result of a stock purchase, with no legal change in the contracting party, and when that contracting party remains in control of the assets and is the party performing the contract.

dod.quote: Restructuring costs are prohibited on novated contracts unless there is an audit of the restructuring proposal; a determination by the contracting officer of overall reduced costs to DoD/NASA; and an Advance Agreement setting forth a cumulative cost ceiling for restructuring projects and the period to which such costs shall be assigned

items.q: Suspension of work versus a stop-work order — which contracts, and what happens to profit?
items.a: A suspension of work applies to construction and architect-engineer contracts; if unreasonable, the contractor may claim increased costs of performance excluding profit. Stop-work orders are for negotiated fixed-price or cost-reimbursement supply, R&D, and service contracts, require approval above the contracting officer, and are never a substitute for a termination notice.

cite.quote: A suspension of work under a construction or architect-engineer contract may be ordered by the contracting officer for a reasonable period of time. If the suspension is unreasonable, the contractor may submit a written claim for increases in the cost of performance, excluding profit.

items.q: A final determination disapproves one of a contractor's business systems. Which systems are covered, and what happens to the contractor's payments?
items.a: Six systems: accounting, earned value management, estimating, material management and accounting, property management, and purchasing. On a final determination with a notice to withhold, the contracting officer withholds 5 percent from progress payments and performance-based payments and directs a 5 percent withhold on interim cost vouchers until all material weaknesses are corrected. An acceptable corrective action plan submitted within 45 days and effectively implemented drops the withhold to 2 percent. Ceilings: 5 percent for material weaknesses in any single system, 10 percent across multiple systems.

cite.quote: the Contracting Officer will withhold 5 percent of amounts due from progress payments and performance-based payments, and direct the Contractor, in writing, to withhold 5 percent from its billings on interim cost vouchers on cost-reimbursement, labor-hour, and time-and-materials contracts

items.q: Are liquidated damages a penalty for late delivery?
items.a: No. They are not punitive and not negative performance incentives — the rate must be a reasonable forecast of just compensation for the harm caused by late delivery or untimely performance, used when timely performance is critical and actual damage would be hard to prove. For DoD construction the liquidated-damages clause (52.211-12) is mandatory in every contract exceeding $900,000 — except cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts or where the contractor cannot control the pace of the work — and optional at or below that figure.

cite.quote: Liquidated damages are not punitive and are not negative performance incentives (see 16.403-2). Liquidated damages are used to compensate the Government for probable damages. Therefore, the liquidated damages rate must be a reasonable forecast of just compensation for the harm that is caused by late delivery or untimely performance of the particular contract.

dod.quote: Insert the clause at FAR 52.211-12, Liquidated Damages—Construction, in all construction contracts exceeding $900,000, except cost-plus-fixed-fee contracts or contracts where the contractor cannot control the pace of the work. Use of the clause in contracts of $900,000 or less is optional.

items.q: What does a contractor get out of a value engineering change proposal?
items.a: A share of the net acquisition savings realized from accepted VECPs, at the clause's incentive sharing rates — contractors are encouraged to submit them voluntarily.

cite.quote: The Contractor is encouraged to develop, prepare, and submit value engineering change proposals (VECP’s) voluntarily. The Contractor shall share in any net acquisition savings realized from accepted VECP’s, in accordance with the incentive sharing rates in paragraph (f) of this clause.

items.q: Who is ordinarily expected to furnish the property needed to perform a Government contract?
items.a: The contractor. The Government provides property only when clearly demonstrated to be in its best interest, the benefit significantly outweighs the administration cost, risk is not substantially increased, and requirements cannot otherwise be met.

cite.quote: Contractors are ordinarily required to furnish all property necessary to perform Government contracts.

items.q: Under which contract types is the contractor generally not held liable for loss of Government property?
items.a: Cost-reimbursement, time-and-material, labor-hour, and fixed-price contracts awarded on the basis of certified cost or pricing data. DoD extends the shield to negotiated fixed-price contracts awarded on a basis other than certified cost or pricing data — so in DoD practice the carve-out reaches essentially every negotiated fixed-price award, leaving sealed-bid fixed-price as the main place full liability survives.

cite.quote: Generally, contractors are not held liable for loss of Government property under the following types of contracts: (1) Cost-reimbursement contracts. (2) Time-and-material contracts. (3) Labor-hour contracts. (4) Fixed-price contracts awarded on the basis of submission of certified cost or pricing data.

dod.quote: In addition to the contract types listed at FAR 45.104, contractors are not held liable for loss of Government property under negotiated fixed-price contracts awarded on a basis other than submission of certified cost or pricing data.

items.q: On a small business set-aside for services, how much may the prime pay to subcontractors that are not similarly situated?
items.a: No more than 50 percent of the amount the Government pays for contract performance. The limit is also 50 percent for supplies (excluding materials), 85 percent for general construction, and 75 percent for special trade construction.

cite.quote: Services (except construction), it will not pay more than 50 percent of the amount paid by the Government for contract performance to subcontractors that are not similarly situated entities.

items.q: What two-part test makes a manufactured end product "domestic" under the Buy American statute?
items.a: The article must be manufactured in the United States, and the cost of domestic components must exceed the applicable content threshold — 60 percent, rising to 65 percent for 2024-2028 deliveries and 75 percent from 2029 (with a separate less-than-5-percent foreign iron and steel rule for predominantly iron or steel products). Per 41 U.S.C. 1907 the domestic content test is waived for COTS items — though not for the iron/steel test, except COTS fasteners. For DoD, the content test counts U.S. and qualifying country components toward the threshold.

cite.quote: The article must be manufactured in the United States; and (2) (i) Except for an end product that consists wholly or predominantly of iron or steel or a combination of both, the cost of domestic components must exceed 60 percent of the cost of all the components, except that the percentage is 65 percent for items delivered in calendar years 2024 through 2028 and 75 percent for items delivered starting in calendar year 2029. But see paragraph (d) of this section. In accordance with 41 U.S.C. 1907, this domestic content test of the Buy American statute has been waived for acquisitions of COTS items (but see paragraph (a)(2)(ii) of this section).

dod.quote: the cost of its U.S. and qualifying country components exceeds 60 percent of the cost of all its components, except that the percentage will be 65 percent for items delivered in calendar years 2024 through 2028 and 75 percent for items delivered starting in calendar year 2029

items.q: What does the Berry Amendment restrict DoD from buying unless it is domestic?
items.a: Items such as food, clothing, tents, cotton and other natural fiber products, wool, canvas products, and hand or measuring tools — they must have been grown, reprocessed, reused, or produced in the United States unless an exception applies.

cite.quote: do not acquire— (1) Any of the following items, either as end products or components, unless the items have been grown, reprocessed, reused, or produced in the United States: (i) Food.

items.q: In an acquisition covered by the WTO Government Procurement Agreement, what end products may be acquired?
items.a: Only U.S.-made or designated country end products (or U.S. or designated country services), unless offers for them are not received or are insufficient to fulfill the requirements. DoD narrows the field twice: trade agreements apply only to end products in the product service groups enumerated at 225.401-70 — if the end product is not in a listed group, the trade agreements do not apply — and in covered acquisitions DoD buys only U.S.-made, qualifying country, or designated country end products unless such offers are not received or are insufficient, or a national interest waiver is granted.

cite.quote: in acquisitions covered by the WTO GPA, acquire only U.S.-made or designated country end products or U.S. or designated country services, unless offers for such end products or services are either not received or are insufficient to fulfill the requirements.

dod.quote: If an end product is not in one of the listed groups, the trade agreements do not apply.

items.q: What contract types must be used for awards resulting from a commercial solutions opening?
items.a: Fixed-price type contracts, including fixed-price incentive. A CSO is a general solicitation for innovative commercial products or services under 10 U.S.C. 3458, and what it buys is treated as commercial.

cite.quote: Notwithstanding FAR 12.104, contracting officers must use fixed-price type contracts, including fixed-price incentive contracts, for awards resulting from a CSO.

items.q: How can a follow-on production contract from an other-transaction prototype project skip a new competition?
items.a: It is excepted from the competition requirements when the OT agreement for the prototype, awarded under 10 U.S.C. 4022, included provisions for a follow-on production contract and the statutory conditions are documented.

cite.quote: Also excepted from this part are follow-on production contracts for products developed pursuant to the “other transactions” authority of 10 U.S.C. 4022 for prototype projects

items.q: What is a multiyear contract, and how does it differ from a contract with options?
items.a: A contract for the purchase of supplies or services for more than 1 but not more than 5 program years — it buys the out-years up front instead of establishing and exercising an option for each program year. Out-year performance may be made contingent on appropriations, and if it is, the contract may provide for a cancellation payment to the contractor; the cancellation ceiling is the maximum charge the contractor can receive. That ceiling caps the Government's liability — it is contractor protection, not Government protection.

cite.quote: Multiyear contract means a contract for the purchase of supplies or services for more than 1, but not more than 5 program years. A multiyear contract may provide that performance under the contract during the second and subsequent years of the contract is contingent upon the appropriation of funds, and (if it does so provide) may provide for a cancellation payment to be made to the contractor if appropriations are not made.

items.q: When is an Earned Value Management System required?
items.a: The civilian baseline is major acquisitions for development, per OMB Circular A-11. DoD replaces that wholesale with thresholds: on cost or incentive contracts, EIA-748 compliance is required at $50 million or more, and at $100 million or more the contractor must have a system the cognizant Federal agency has validated against EIA-748. Below $50 million, applying EVM is optional and a risk-based decision; on firm-fixed-price contracts of any value it is discouraged (waiver procedures apply); and the subpart does not apply to contracts primarily for software.

cite.quote: In accordance with OMB Circular A-11, agencies must require an Earned Value Management System (EVMS) in major acquisitions for development.

dod.quote: For cost or incentive contracts and subcontracts valued at $50 million or more, the clause at 252.234-7999, Earned Value Management System, requires the contractor’s earned value management system to comply with the guidelines in Electronic Industries Alliance Standard 748, Earned Value Management Systems
